//: What replaces what. Data rather than code, so it grows without a rebuild.
//1: A type mapped to null is a recorded fact: nothing in the new package does its job.
//2: A type absent from this file is unknown, which is not the same as fine.

Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.note: The pipeline, the routing and the filters all change shape. Most types have a counterpart, and the controllers still have to be moved onto the new hosting model.

types.//sibling: ASP.NET Core split MVC across several packages, so a counterpart is not always inside Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc. These are recorded with where they live, because a name in a sibling package looks the same from a namespace as a coincidence does, and they were being left in the column nobody had looked at.
types.//trap: System.Web.HttpContext is deliberately absent from this list. It has a namesake in Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http and they share a word and nothing else, which is the case that makes naming a namespace a bad way to decide.

removed.//: Deleted rather than replaced: the framework withdrew the feature, so there is nothing left for the use to do. Different from a type mapped to null, which leaves somebody with a problem.
removed.AllowHtml: Turns off ASP.NET's request validation for one property. ASP.NET Core has no request validation, so there is nothing to turn off. Delete the attribute; the model binder does not reject markup.
removed.ValidateInput: The same feature at action or controller level. ASP.NET Core never inspects a request for markup, so nothing has to be allowed through.
removed.JsonRequestBehavior: Existed to refuse JSON over GET, against a hijacking attack the framework no longer treats this way. ASP.NET Core's Json() takes no such argument and the call site loses the parameter.

observed.//: Read off finished migrations rather than written from knowledge. Each name kept its name and changed namespace, and the framework was asked whether the successor really contains it.

Microsoft.AspNet.WebApi.Core.note: Web API and MVC are one framework on ASP.NET Core. A controller stops deriving from ApiController and derives from ControllerBase, and the action results are the MVC ones. The routing attributes keep their names and change namespace, and the configuration object has no counterpart because configuration is services and middleware now.

Microsoft.AspNet.WebApi.WebHost.note: It hosted Web API inside IIS through System.Web. ASP.NET Core is its own host and there is nothing to configure in its place: the reference goes and the hosting is Program.cs.

Microsoft.AspNet.Razor.note: The engine itself is not a public API anybody ports. Views move with MVC and the syntax is the same. Code that drove the engine directly, to render a template outside a request, is a different question and is asked as one.

Owin.note: Katana is the .NET Framework host. ASP.NET Core has its own pipeline and does not run it, so an OWIN startup class becomes middleware in Program.cs rather than being ported.

Microsoft.AspNet.WebPages.note: No direct successor. Razor itself carries over, the WebPages hosting model does not, and anything built on it is a rewrite rather than a replacement.

Microsoft.AspNet.Web.Optimization.note: Nothing in ASP.NET Core replaces it, and the need it served does not go away with it: the assets still have to be bundled somewhere. That is the difference between this and a feature the framework withdrew, and it is why every type here is recorded as having no counterpart rather than as deleted.

Microsoft.Web.Infrastructure.note: Nothing replaces it because nothing needs to. It existed to register modules at run time under System.Web, which modern .NET does not have. Remove the reference.

Newtonsoft.Json.note: In the framework, faster, and stricter. The strictness is the migration: trailing commas, comments, case-insensitive names and number-as-string all have to be turned on deliberately, and JObject has no counterpart worth pretending about.

log4net.note: The abstraction is in the framework and the appenders are not. Configuration moves from XML to code or to appsettings, and the hierarchy of named loggers becomes categories.
Closer to log4net in spirit, with sinks in place of appenders and structured properties rather than formatted strings. A third-party dependency where the other option is in the framework.
